title: Breaker Blocks: Trading Failed Order Blocks
quickAnswer: A breaker block is a failed order block whose polarity flips after price sweeps an external swing high or low (Point A to C) and then closes decisively through the opposing swing (Point B to D). Once broken on a closing basis, the old candle range at Point B becomes a reference from the opposite side—acting as potential support in a bullish breaker or resistance in a bearish breaker—with highest structural clarity when overlapped by a positive-width Fair Value Gap (the ICT Unicorn model).

sections.title: What Is a Breaker Block? The Beginner Mental Model

extract.name: Breaker Block Definition
extract.text: A breaker block is a previously valid order-block candle or consecutive candle run that fails to hold after price sweeps a prior external swing and subsequently closes through the intervening structure, reversing the reference zone from resistance to support (bullish breaker) or from support to resistance (bearish breaker).

paragraphs: Imagine walking up a staircase onto a glass floor that looks sturdy enough to hold your weight. Suddenly the floor cracks, you drop to the level below, and when you look back up, that exact same glass pane is now the ceiling above your head. In Smart Money Concepts (SMC) and Inner Circle Trader (ICT) price action, that floor-to-ceiling or ceiling-to-floor role flip is the core intuition behind a breaker block.

Every trader who has studied standard order blocks has watched a clean-looking candle zone get smashed straight through instead of bouncing. Beginners usually erase that broken rectangle in frustration. Experienced price-action analysts do the opposite: they check whether the market first swept an earlier swing high or low before shattering the order block. When both events happen in chronological order, the failed order block is promoted into a breaker block.

Unlike generic support-and-resistance flips drawn anywhere on a chart, a true breaker block requires an observable four-point swing sequence (A, B, C, and D) before the retest arrives. That strict sequence separates genuine structural role reversals from random lines drawn after hindsight reveals a bounce.
bullets: Old floor cracks -> becomes new overhead ceiling (Bearish Breaker Block).
Old ceiling shatters -> becomes new underfoot floor (Bullish Breaker Block).
Requires an external sweep past Point A followed by a closing break past Point B before any valid retest.

callout.label: Core Mental Anchor
callout.text: A breaker block is not just any broken rectangle. It is a specific order-block origin that fails right after an external liquidity sweep, turning the old breakout zone into an opposing retest reference.

sections.title: The 4-Point A–B–C–D Sequence & Polarity Flip Mechanics
paragraphs: To identify a breaker block objectively on any candlestick chart—whether Nasdaq futures (NQ), EUR/USD, Gold (XAU/USD), or Bitcoin—trace four chronological structural events labeled A, B, C, and D. Skipping or reordering any step turns the setup into a different pattern.

First, the market prints an initial swing extreme at Point A. Second, price retraces to create an opposing swing at Point B—this is where the origin candle (the initial order block) sits. Third, price drives back past Point A to print Point C, sweeping resting stops beyond the old swing. Fourth, instead of continuing, price reverses energetically and produces a completed candle body close past Point B at Point D (a Market Structure Shift, or MSS).

Only after Point D closes past Point B does the saved candle range at Point B officially qualify as a breaker block. Any touch of Point B before candle D closes is premature and does not count as a valid breaker retest.
numberedPoints: Event A (Initial Reference Swing): Establishes the external high (bearish case) or external low (bullish case) where stop orders accumulate.
Event B (Origin Candle / Failed Order Block): The intervening swing whose final opposing candle or consecutive run launches the sweep into C.
Event C (External Liquidity Sweep): Price trades strictly beyond Point A, triggering breakout entries and protective stops.
Event D (Confirmed Body-Close MSS): Displacement closes decisively beyond Point B, invalidating the original order block and activating its opposite polarity.
Event E (Optional Retest): Price later returns to the saved Point B range from the new side—where three outcomes remain possible: hold, closing failure, or no retest.

sections.title: Bullish vs. Bearish Breaker Blocks: Mirroring Structure Correctly
paragraphs: A common beginner mistake is memorizing the bullish diagram and flipping only the arrows when scanning a downtrend. Bullish and bearish breaker blocks are exact structural mirrors, which means their sweep direction, origin candle polarity, retest approach, and invalidation boundaries invert completely.

In a Bullish Breaker Block, price establishes a Low (A), rallies to a High (B), drops below A to form a Lower Low sweep (C), and then surges upward to close above High B (D). The breaker zone is anchored to the last up-close candle (or consecutive up-close run) at High B that originally tried to act as bearish resistance. Once price closes above it, that former ceiling is studied from above as bullish support.

In a Bearish Breaker Block, price establishes a High (A), pulls back to a Low (B), rallies above A to form a Higher High sweep (C), and then collapses downward to close below Low B (D). The breaker zone is anchored to the last down-close candle (or consecutive down-close run) at Low B that originally tried to hold as bullish support. Once price closes below it, that former floor is studied from below as bearish resistance.
bullets: Bullish Mirror: Sweep below Low A (C) -> body close above High B (D) -> save last up-close candle/run at B -> retest from above.
Bearish Mirror: Sweep above High A (C) -> body close below Low B (D) -> save last down-close candle/run at B -> retest from below.

sections.title: Exact OHLC Marking Conventions: Opening Price, Body, Full Range & Mean Threshold

extract.name: Breaker Block Mean Threshold Formula
extract.formula: Body Mean Threshold = (Body_Low + Body_High) / 2   |   Full-Range Mean Threshold = (Candle_Low + Candle_High) / 2
extract.text: The 50% Mean Threshold divides the chosen breaker reference into an upper and lower half. In standard breaker-block conventions, closing past the 50% Mean Threshold signals structural weakening even before the outer wick extreme breaks.

paragraphs: Ask five traders on TradingView to draw the same breaker block and you will often see three slightly different rectangles. That ambiguity disappears when you lock a single OHLC marking convention before the retest occurs and document it in your playbook.

Whichever boundary convention you test—body-only or full-range—never switch mid-trade after seeing where a wick turned. Changing from body to wick in hindsight creates an illusion of precision that cannot be replicated live.
numberedPoints: Opening Price (Proximal Edge): The opening print of the first opposing candle in the Point B candle or consecutive run.
Body Range (Open to Close): The solid open-to-close core excluding erratic news wicks.
Full Range (High to Low): The complete wick-to-wick envelope marking the outer structural invalidation boundary.
50% Mean Threshold (Midpoint): The exact arithmetic halfway coordinate of the chosen body or full range.

sections.title: Single Candle vs. Consecutive Run & The Wick-vs.-Body Violation Rule
paragraphs: Two practical questions dominate trader forums and YouTube comments: first, should a breaker block cover only the single last opposing candle at Point B or the entire consecutive run of same-colored candles? Second, does a long wick piercing Point B count as a confirmed breaker flip, or must the candle body close beyond it?

On consecutive runs: when two or three same-direction candles print back-to-back at Point B without an intervening opposite candle, treating the combined consecutive run as one composite block preserves the true start of that price leg (its opening price) and prevents cherry-picking whichever single candle looks cleanest after the fact. When the last candle alone already contains an unusually large range, some intraday models narrow focus to that final candle—just declare the rule ahead of time.

On wick versus body close: a wick spiking past Point B and snapping back inside the old range is a liquidity probe, not a verified structural flip. Requiring a completed candle body close beyond Point B (on your breaker timeframe) filters out the majority of false breakouts and premature role-reversal traps.
bullets: Consecutive Run Rule: Group adjacent same-color candles at Point B into one composite block to lock the true leg open.
Body-Close Confirmation Rule: Wicks sweep liquidity (Point A -> C); completed candle bodies confirm structural shifts (Point B -> D).

callout.label: Non-Negotiable Verification Rule
callout.text: Wicks sweep liquidity (Point A to C); candle bodies confirm structure (Point B to D). If Point D only wicks past Point B and closes back inside, wait for a genuine closing break before calling the zone a breaker.

sections.title: Trapped-Participant Narrative vs. Observable OHLC Evidence
paragraphs: Most online guides explain breaker blocks with a dramatic story: large players push price past Point A to trap retail breakout traders, reverse the market through Point B, and then bring price back to Point B so they can close underwater positions at breakeven before driving price to the real target.

That trapped-participant narrative is an intuitive memory aid for why polarity flips often attract volume near Point B. However, an honest educator must draw a bright line between a plausible market-microstructure hypothesis and what an OHLC candlestick chart can actually prove.

A candlestick chart shows open, high, low, close, and time. It does not reveal trader identities, bank order tickets, or whether a specific participant exited at breakeven. What we can verify objectively is narrower and far more useful for repeatable research.
bullets: Observable Fact: Price exceeded Point A, then produced a completed closing break beyond Point B.
Observable Fact: The Point B candle range and 50% Mean Threshold can be measured identically by two independent analysts before the retest.
Unverified Hypothesis: Assuming every single breaker retest represents a specific desk mitigating a losing hedging leg at exact breakeven.
Practical Benefit: Trading the observable geometry with fixed stop rules works regardless of which mix of participants or breakout stops created the move.

sections.title: Breaker Block vs. Order Block vs. Mitigation Block vs. Propulsion Block
paragraphs: Half of the confusion in Smart Money Concepts comes from mixing up four cousin PD arrays that look similar at a glance: Order Blocks, Breaker Blocks, Mitigation Blocks, and Propulsion Blocks. Each one occupies a completely different structural position in a price swing.
Inspect the interactive four-way structural comparator below to see each geometry side by side.
numberedPoints: Order Block (OB): An unbroken origin candle tested from its original side for trend continuation.
Breaker Block (BB): A broken origin candle preceded by an external liquidity sweep beyond Point A (polarity flip).
Mitigation Block (MB): A broken origin candle where Point C failed to sweep Point A (failure swing without an external raid).
Propulsion Block (PB): A secondary continuation candle that dips into an existing parent Order Block and launches accelerated expansion.

sections.title: The ICT Unicorn Model: Breaker Block + Fair Value Gap Overlap

extract.name: ICT Unicorn Overlap Formula
extract.formula: Unicorn_Low = max(BB_Low, FVG_Low)   |   Unicorn_High = min(BB_High, FVG_High)   |   Valid iff Unicorn_High > Unicorn_Low
extract.text: An ICT Unicorn setup occurs only when a confirmed Breaker Block and a same-direction displacement Fair Value Gap share a strictly positive-width price intersection (Unicorn_High > Unicorn_Low).

paragraphs: Among all breaker variations searched on Google and YouTube, the ICT Unicorn Model is by far the most famous. Rather than trading a wide breaker block blindly, the Unicorn model waits for the displacement leg that breaks Point B (producing Point D) to simultaneously leave behind a clean three-candle Fair Value Gap (FVG) that physically overlaps the saved Breaker Block range.

Why does that overlap matter geometrically? Because the breaker defines where structural polarity flipped, while the overlapping Fair Value Gap proves that displacement through Point B happened with genuine speed and an observable three-candle price imbalance. The intersection shrinks a broad breaker zone into a crisp, narrower target window for study.

Crucially, an overlapping breaker and FVG originate from the same impulsive sequence—they are not two independent market votes, nor does the Unicorn name supply an automatic edge without higher-timeframe bias, liquidity draw, and strict risk control.
numberedPoints: Step 1 — Save Origin B: Freeze the Breaker Block range before the impulsive break completes.
Step 2 — Confirm Sweep & Displacement Break: Point C sweeps Point A, then a fast displacement leg closes past Point B leaving a 3-candle Fair Value Gap.
Step 3 — Verify Positive-Width Overlap: Confirm Unicorn_High > Unicorn_Low before studying any retest into the narrowed overlap window.

sections.title: Interactive Unicorn Overlap Calculator & Zero-Width Boundary Traps
paragraphs: Many traders label any breaker that sits merely near an FVG as a Unicorn. Mathematically, proximity and overlap are completely different states. If a bearish breaker spans 100.00–104.00 and a bearish FVG spans 104.00–106.00, the two intervals touch at the single point 104.00—producing an overlap width of 0.00. Touching edges do not form a positive-width Unicorn zone.

Experiment with the interactive calculator below by sliding the Breaker Block and FVG boundaries. Watch how the intersection transitions cleanly between a Positive-Width Unicorn Overlap, a Zero-Width Touching Edge, and a Disjoint Gap, and check whether the FVG's 50% Consequent Encroachment (CE) lands inside or outside the overlap.

sections.title: Inverse Breakers (Reclaimed / Failed Breakers): When Polarity Flips Twice
paragraphs: What happens when a textbook breaker block fails on a closing basis? Beginners panic and discard the chart, whereas advanced tape readers recognize an Inverse Breaker (also called a Reclaimed Breaker or Failed Breaker continuation).

Suppose a Bearish Breaker forms at 100.00–104.00 after a buy-side sweep, suggesting lower prices. Instead of rejecting, buyers drive straight through 104.00 and close decisively above the breaker's upper boundary. That closing failure reveals that the earlier sell-off was merely an intraday shakeout inside a stronger higher-timeframe uptrend.

Once price closes back above 104.00, the failed Bearish Breaker reverts to bullish support on a subsequent pullback—meaning the zone flipped polarity twice (Support -> Bearish Breaker -> Reclaimed Bullish Support). In practice, failed breakers inside an opposing higher-timeframe trend are one of the clearest warnings to stop fighting the dominant order flow.
numberedPoints: Phase 1 (Initial Support): Origin candle at 100.00–104.00 launches the buy-side rally.
Phase 2 (First Flip — Bearish Breaker): Sellers close below 100.00, turning 100.00–104.00 into potential resistance.
Phase 3 (Closing Failure): Strong buyers close decisively above 104.00, invalidating the Bearish Breaker thesis.
Phase 4 (Second Flip — Reclaimed Bullish Support): Pullbacks into 100.00–104.00 from above are studied as trend continuation.

callout.label: Double-Flip Diagnostic
callout.text: When a clean LTF breaker fails immediately on a strong closing candle against the HTF trend, treat the failure as valuable directional evidence rather than immediately hunting another counter-trend breaker.

sections.title: High-Probability vs. Low-Probability Breaker Blocks
paragraphs: Because price prints dozens of tiny A–B–C–D swings every day on 1-minute and 5-minute charts, trading every breaker mechanically leads to overtrading and chop. High-probability breaker study filters out random mid-range noise by demanding alignment across location, liquidity, displacement, and session timing.

The single biggest separator is where Point C occurs. A sweep of a major higher-timeframe pool—such as Previous Day High/Low (PDH/PDL), Asia Session High/Low, London Session extreme, or clean equal highs/lows—carries dramatically more structural weight than a sweep of an obscure three-candle micro-swing in the middle of a lunch consolidation.
bullets: High-Probability Filter: Major HTF/session sweep + energetic body-close MSS + overlapping FVG + active Killzone + fresh first retest.
Low-Probability Trap: Minor midday chop sweep + weak creeping break + oversized news wick + third or fourth pass through the same box.

sections.title: Killzone Timing & Liquidity Draw Alignment (America/New_York)
paragraphs: Price geometry without time context loses half its explanatory power. In equities index futures (NQ, ES) and major FX pairs (EUR/USD, GBP/USD), centralized futures and FX venues experience scheduled volume surges at recurring session opens measured on the New York clock (America/New_York, observing seasonal EST/EDT daylight saving shifts).

Always identify the opposing Draw on Liquidity (DOL)—the resting external pool where price has room to travel—before measuring a breaker retest. A textbook breaker formed two ticks away from a major opposing HTF swing has nowhere left to expand.
numberedPoints: London Killzone (02:00–05:00 NY): Frequent Point C sweeps of the overnight Asian Range High or Low.
NY AM Killzone & Silver Bullet (08:30–11:00 NY): Spans 08:30 macro releases, the 09:30 NYSE cash open, and the 10:00–11:00 continuation window.
NY PM Session (13:30–16:00 NY): Afternoon sweeps of the NY Lunch range (12:00–13:30) that often form continuation breakers.

sections.title: Invalidation Rules, Stop Placement, Intrabar Risk & Three Endings
paragraphs: Every qualified breaker block ends in one of three distinct empirical outcomes, and beginners routinely confuse closing-based pattern invalidation with intrabar stop-loss execution. Explore all three endings and all three stop-placement tiers interactively below.
numberedPoints: Ending 1 — Retest & Hold: Price enters the saved Point B zone, respects the closing boundary, and expands toward opposing liquidity.
Ending 2 — Closing Failure: Price closes decisively beyond the far edge of the breaker, invalidating the polarity flip (and potentially launching an Inverse Breaker).
Ending 3 — No Retest / Runaway: Price expands straight to the target without returning before your session expiry window closes.
bullets: Aggressive Stop Tier: Placed just beyond the overlapping FVG / 50% Mean Threshold (tightest distance, higher intrabar wick-out rate).
Structural Stop Tier: Placed beyond the distal outer wick of the Breaker Block (balanced structural standard).
Wide Swing Stop Tier: Placed beyond the Point C sweep extreme (widest protection, smallest position size for equal capital risk).

Execution Rule (SEC Investor.gov): Never widen a stop after entry, define a time-based expiry, and remember stop-market orders can slip during fast news while stop-limit orders risk remaining unfilled in a gap.

sections.title: Authoritative Breaker Block Glossary (22 Terms)
paragraphs: Every technical phrase used across modern SMC and breaker-block chart literature is defined cleanly below with exact structural boundaries so beginners and experienced reviewers share one unambiguous vocabulary.

glossaryTerms.definition: A failed order block whose polarity flips after an external swing sweep (Point C beyond A) and a completed body-close structural break through Point B.
The last up-close candle or consecutive up-close run at an intervening swing high (B) that flips to potential support after price sweeps a prior low (A->C) and closes above B.
The last down-close candle or consecutive down-close run at an intervening swing low (B) that flips to potential resistance after price sweeps a prior high (A->C) and closes below B.
The structural transition in which a former resistance reference is studied as support, or a former support reference is studied as resistance, after a verified closing break.
Price trading strictly beyond a preselected prior swing high (buy-side liquidity) or swing low (sell-side liquidity) at Point C before reversing.
An energetic directional break where a candle body closes decisively past the intervening swing (Point B), qualifying the breaker flip.
The exact halfway coordinate of a breaker block's body range or full high-to-low range; body closes past it warn of weakening structural support or resistance.
The proximal opening price of the first opposing candle in the saved Point B candle or consecutive run, often used as an early retest benchmark.
Two or more back-to-back same-color candles forming the origin leg at Point B, treated as one unified composite breaker zone.
An intrabar excursion that pokes beyond Point B but closes back inside the prior range, failing to satisfy a body-close MSS rule.
A confluence structure where a confirmed Breaker Block shares a strictly positive-width price intersection with a same-direction displacement Fair Value Gap.
An overlap interval [max(BB_Low, FVG_Low), min(BB_High, FVG_High)] where the upper edge is strictly greater than the lower edge (width > 0).
Two adjacent zones meeting at a single shared boundary price (width = 0), which does not constitute a true overlapping Unicorn zone.
A failed-swing structure that breaks Point B after Point C fails to sweep Point A (forming a lower high in bearish structure or higher low in bullish structure).
A secondary continuation candle that dips into an existing parent Order Block and launches accelerated expansion in the original trend direction.
A qualified breaker block that fails on a decisive closing basis and flips polarity a second time, resuming the pre-sweep directional trend.
The exact 50% midpoint of a Fair Value Gap, frequently compared against the breaker's Mean Threshold inside a Unicorn intersection.
The opposing resting swing high, swing low, or session extreme toward which price has structural room to expand after a breaker retest.
A scheduled high-volume trading period measured on America/New_York local time (such as London 02:00–05:00 or NY AM 08:30–11:00).
Energetic, large-bodied directional price expansion through Point B that leaves visible three-candle Fair Value Gaps and signals strong conviction.
A predefined completed candle body close beyond the distal edge of the breaker block that invalidates the structural polarity thesis.
A protective stop-order fill caused by a transient wick excursion beyond the stop price even if the candle later closes back inside the breaker.

sections.title: Baseline Curriculum Reference Retention & Primary Sources
paragraphs: To preserve continuity with earlier LearnSMC syllabus citations and bilingual study reviews, all twenty-two original baseline reference paragraphs from Chapter 16 (Price Delivery Edition, Sections 16.1–16.7) are retained verbatim below alongside the expanded modern framework.

baselineSections.heading: What changes when an old reference fails?
paragraphs: The previous lesson saved a candle-based reference before price returned to it. A breaker study follows what happens when price travels through a saved reference and later approaches it from the opposite side. The important feature is the surrounding swing sequence, not simply a box changing colour.

In a bearish example, price trades above an earlier high, reverses, and then breaks the intervening low. A saved candle area near that low can become a reference on a later rally. In a bullish example, price trades below an earlier low, reverses, and breaks the intervening high; a later decline approaches the saved area from above.

“Trapped buyers” and “trapped sellers” are common explanations for such reversals. They are hypotheses about participants. The observable lesson is narrower: a reference was crossed, a swing sequence changed, and price may or may not return. We can teach and test that sequence without pretending to see every trader’s position.

baselineSections.heading: Bearish breaker: follow A, B, C and D in time
paragraphs: Start with four labelled events. A is a high at 110. Price falls to B, a low at 100. It rallies to C, a higher high at 112, trading beyond A. It then reverses and produces D, a completed close at 98 below B. The sweep of A and the later break of B are separate events; C alone is not the completed bearish sequence.

For this illustration, save the up-close candle at B that launched the rally: open 101, high 104, low 100, close 103. Its full range is 100–104. After the close below B, extend that saved range forward. A rally to 103 is now an approach from below into the reference.

This is an explicitly stated drawing convention for the example. Candle/run selection and body-versus-wick boundaries vary across models and chart timeframes. Do not turn a candle-colour shortcut into a universal definition, and do not select a different candle after seeing the retest. The diagram makes the chosen candle and qualification time visible.

baselineSections.heading: Bullish breaker: reverse the structure, not just the arrows
paragraphs: The bullish mirror begins with A, a low at 100, then B, a high at 110. Price falls to C at 98, below A, and subsequently closes at D at 112, above B. The lower low comes first; the upward structural break follows.

In this illustration, the selected down-close candle at B opens at 109, reaches a high of 110 and low of 106, and closes at 107. Save its full range of 106–110. After the upward break, a decline to 108 approaches that area from above. The expected role in the study has reversed, but a reaction is still uncertain.

Check the mirror carefully. A bearish reference is approached on a rally from below; a bullish reference is approached on a decline from above. Their adverse sides and hypothetical stop locations are opposite. Merely recolouring the same chart can conceal a direction error.

baselineSections.heading: Breaker block vs. mitigation block: what is the difference?
paragraphs: A useful teaching distinction compares two nearly identical bearish sequences. In the breaker illustration, A is 110, B is 100 and C reaches 112 before the break below B. C takes the earlier high. In the comparison, C reaches only 108 before price breaks below B; it fails to exceed A.

The second path is often described as a mitigation-block structure: a failed swing followed by a break, without the same external-high sweep in this comparison. This terminology is not used consistently by every educator. State the actual highs, lows and selection rule rather than relying on a label to carry the whole explanation.

Also distinguish “mitigation block” from the verb “mitigate.” The previous chapter used mitigation for a return to a saved order-block reference. That return alone does not create the failed-swing structure shown here. Similar vocabulary can describe different parts of a chart.

baselineSections.heading: What is a Unicorn setup, and how do you measure the overlap?
paragraphs: A Unicorn setup is commonly taught as a breaker reference overlapping a same-direction FVG in an appropriate sequence. It is not any order block beside any gap. Both references must qualify under the chosen model before the decision that uses them.

Take the bearish breaker range 100–104 and a separately completed bearish FVG at 102–106. The shared interval begins at the larger lower boundary, 102, and ends at the smaller upper boundary, 104. Their overlap is 102–104. The FVG’s midpoint is 104; that happens to sit on the overlap’s upper edge, not at its centre.

Now move the FVG to 104–106. The intervals touch at 104 but share no positive-width area. Move it to 105–107 and there is no intersection at all. Proximity and overlap are different. For the bullish mirror, a breaker at 106–110 and FVG at 104–108 overlap at 106–108.

Overlapping drawings are not independent votes from separate markets. They can arise from the same candles. Whether the combination improves a particular strategy requires a defined sample and comparison; the name supplies no verified win rate.

baselineSections.heading: Retest, response and failure: three different endings
paragraphs: After the bearish structural break, price may rally into 100–104 and turn downward. It may instead close above 104, failing a rule that requires the full range to hold on a closing basis. Or it may continue downward without ever returning before the idea expires. Those are three distinct endings, not three ways to describe the same successful setup.

Choose when the observation starts and ends. A touch before the structural break is not a qualified retest of the completed sequence. A retest after an arbitrary expiry should not be counted as an eligible entry just because the reaction later looks attractive.

For this illustration, a short paper entry at 103, stop at 105 and target at 99 has 2 points of planned risk and 4 of reward: 2R before costs. A high of 105 can trigger the protective stop even if the candle later closes below 104. The trade can lose while the closing-based pattern rule remains intact. Neither rule may be rewritten after the result.

baselineSections.heading: How FVG, IFVG, order blocks and breakers fit together
paragraphs: Use the four lessons as different lenses. FVG describes a three-candle interval. IFVG studies an opposite-role use after that completed interval is crossed under a stated rule. An order block selects a candle or run associated with a departure. A breaker adds a role reversal within a specified swing sequence; a Unicorn studies its intersection with a qualifying FVG.

The same price movement can produce more than one of these references. That does not make them synonyms or prove a trade is strong. Ask what each drawing adds: a measurable interval, a timing condition, a swing reference, or a different boundary. If two labels add no new information, avoid counting them twice.

For practice, pause a chart before the retest, label A–D, save the selected candle and calculate any overlap. Predict nothing. Advance one candle, record what became known, and keep the failed and absent returns. This habit turns a memorable pattern into a study you can explain to another learner.

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions About Breaker Blocks
paragraphs: Direct, concise answers to the twelve most frequently searched questions about bullish and bearish breaker blocks, mitigation comparisons, Unicorn overlaps, wick-versus-body rules, and invalidation.

faqs.q: What is a breaker block in trading?
faqs.a: A breaker block is a failed order block whose polarity reverses after price sweeps an earlier swing high or low (Point A to C) and then closes decisively past the intervening swing (Point B to D). Once broken on a closing basis, the saved candle range at Point B is studied from the opposite side as potential support (bullish breaker) or resistance (bearish breaker).

faqs.q: What is the exact difference between an Order Block and a Breaker Block?
faqs.a: An Order Block is an unbroken origin candle tested from its original side for continuation. A Breaker Block is an Order Block that failed and broke on a closing basis following an external liquidity sweep, causing its expected role to invert from resistance to support or from support to resistance.

faqs.q: How is a Breaker Block different from a Mitigation Block?
faqs.a: A Breaker Block requires Point C to trade strictly beyond Point A (an external liquidity sweep) before price reverses and breaks Point B. A Mitigation Block occurs when Point C fails to reach Point A—printing a lower high in a bearish shift or a higher low in a bullish shift—before breaking Point B.

faqs.q: How do you identify a Bullish Breaker Block step by step?
faqs.a: Mark Swing Low A, then intervening Swing High B (saving its last up-close candle or consecutive up-close run). Wait for price to drop below A to create a Lower Low sweep at C, then surge upward with a completed candle body close strictly above High B (Point D). On a later pullback into the saved B range from above, study it as a Bullish Breaker.

faqs.q: How do you identify a Bearish Breaker Block step by step?
faqs.a: Mark Swing High A, then intervening Swing Low B (saving its last down-close candle or consecutive down-close run). Wait for price to rally above A to create a Higher High sweep at C, then reverse downward with a completed candle body close strictly below Low B (Point D). On a later rally into the saved B range from below, study it as a Bearish Breaker.

faqs.q: Should I draw a Breaker Block using candle bodies, wicks, or consecutive candles?
faqs.a: Both body-only (open-to-close) and full-range (high-to-low) conventions are used, and consecutive same-color candles at Point B are commonly grouped into one composite block. The critical discipline is choosing one convention before the retest and logging its 50% Mean Threshold consistently—never redrawing the box after seeing the bounce.

faqs.q: Does a wick past Point B confirm a Breaker Block, or do I need a body close?
faqs.a: A wick-only spike past Point B that closes back inside the old range is a liquidity probe, not a confirmed structural flip. Waiting for a completed candle body close strictly beyond Point B (Point D) filters out most false breakouts.

faqs.q: What is the ICT Unicorn Model and how is the overlap measured?
faqs.a: The ICT Unicorn Model pairs a confirmed Breaker Block with a same-direction displacement Fair Value Gap that overlaps it. Measure the overlap from max(BB_Low, FVG_Low) to min(BB_High, FVG_High); the setup qualifies only when the upper boundary is strictly greater than the lower boundary (positive width, not merely touching edges).

faqs.q: What is the 50% Mean Threshold of a Breaker Block?
faqs.a: The Mean Threshold is the arithmetic 50% midpoint of the breaker's selected body or full range. Traders often watch how candle bodies react around this midpoint; a decisive body close past 50% warns that the breaker's polarity flip is weakening.

faqs.q: What is an Inverse Breaker or Reclaimed Breaker?
faqs.a: An Inverse (or Reclaimed) Breaker occurs when a qualified breaker fails on a decisive candle body close through its far edge. That double role-flip signals that the pre-sweep trend has reclaimed control, and the failed breaker zone often acts in its original pre-sweep direction again.

faqs.q: Where do traders place stop losses and what invalidates a Breaker Block?
faqs.a: Structural invalidation occurs when a candle body closes decisively past the distal edge of the breaker (below the low for a bullish breaker, or above the high for a bearish breaker). Protective stops are typically evaluated beyond the breaker's outer edge or beyond the Point C sweep, keeping in mind that intrabar wicks and spread widening can trigger stops before a candle closes.

faqs.q: Which markets and timeframes work best for studying Breaker Blocks?
faqs.a: Breaker geometry is fractal and appears across futures (NQ, ES), major FX pairs (EUR/USD, GBP/USD), commodities (Gold), and liquid crypto markets. Many learners pair a Daily/4H directional bias with a 15-minute or 5-minute breaker formed during the London (02:00–05:00 NY) or New York AM (08:30–11:00 NY) Killzones.
